title: Paraeus, Ames, British: prior conditions, not causing causes
source_text: LIII. Qua de re videri potest Paraeus in Bellarminum lib. 5. de Justif. cap. 7. Secundo, inquit, tenendum est, non esse idem dicere dispositiones praecedere justifica-tionem, seu requiri ante justificationem, & dispositiones requiri ad justificationem, seu justificationem acquiri per dispositiones. Nos posterius negamus. Prius recte intelle-ctum concedimus. Similiter Amesius in Bellarmino Enervato, Tom. 4. lib. 5. cap. 4. responsione ad quartum argumentum, concedit dilectionem aliquam esse priorem remis-sione peccatorum, sive justificatione, ut conditionem praerequisitam; licet dilectio nulla remissionem praecedat ut dispositio causans. Et resp. ad quintum argumentum, poenitentia quae est dolor & detestatio peccati, ipso fatente antecedit quidem justifi-cationem, ut dispositio ex ordine praerequisita; sed non ut causa. Quibuscum con-sentiunt quae Theol. Britanni in judicio jam citato dicunt. Ad statum justificationis, in quo pacem habemus apud Deum per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum, non solet gratia divina homines perducere per subitum enthusiastum, sed multis praeviis actio-nibus ministerio Verbi subactos, & praeparatos. Hoc videre licet in illis, qui audita Petri concione, peccati onus sentiunt, timent, dolent, liberationem desiderant, spem ali-quam veniae concipiunt: quae omnia ex illis verbis concipi possunt, Act. 2. 37. Quum haec audivissent, compuncti sunt corde suo, & dixerunt ad Petrum & reliquos Apo-stolos, Viri Fratres, quid faciemus?
pass_a_gloss: On which matter Paraeus on Bellarmine, book 5 on Justification, chapter 7, may be seen. Secondly, he says, it is to be held that it is not the same to say that dispositions precede justification, or are required before justification, and that dispositions are required for justification, or that justification is acquired through dispositions. We deny the latter. The former, rightly understood, we concede. Likewise Ames in Bellarmine Enervated, volume 4, book 5, chapter 4, in the reply to the fourth argument, concedes that some love is prior to the remission of sins or justification as a prerequisite condition; although no love precedes remission as a causing disposition. And in the reply to the fifth argument, repentance which is sorrow and detestation of sin, he himself confessing, indeed precedes justification as a disposition prerequisite by order, but not as a cause. With which agree what the British theologians say in the judgment already cited: To the state of justification, in which we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, divine grace is not accustomed to bring men by a sudden enthusiasm, but men subdued and prepared by many prior actions through the ministry of the Word. This may be seen in those who, having heard Peter's sermon, feel the burden of sin, fear, grieve, desire deliverance, conceive some hope of pardon: all which can be gathered from those words, Acts 2:37: When they heard these things, they were pricked in their heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, Men and brethren, what shall we do?
pass_b_english: Paraeus: dispositions may precede justification; justification is not acquired by them as causes.
Ames and the British: prior conditions under the Word, not sudden enthusiasm—Acts 2:37.
